options.text: Keep all rows in the table, add disk, and retune autovacuum for it

options.name: partdrop
options.text: Convert to monthly partitions, detach old ones, and export them to object storage

options.name: batchdelete
options.text: Archive rows older than 90 days to files and delete them in nightly batches

decision: Where should the team run its 9 containerized services?
context: Nine services handle 300 requests a second at peak, and 5 engineers share on-call. Nobody has operated Kubernetes in production, though two engineers used it at previous jobs. The company expects to double the service count within 18 months.

options.name: hostedpaas
options.text: A hosted platform that builds and deploys each service from its repository

options.name: vmsystemd
options.text: Virtual machines running containers under systemd, with Ansible roles and a load balancer

options.name: managedkube
options.text: A managed Kubernetes cluster, with a Helm chart and namespace for each service

options.name: containersvc
options.text: A cloud provider container service that runs each task without node management

decision: How should infrastructure-as-code changes reach production?
context: 12 engineers merge 15 infrastructure changes a week across 3 environments, and last year a console edit that drifted from the code caused one 40-minute outage. Plans take 12 minutes to compute, and only 3 senior engineers hold production credentials today.

options.name: nightly
options.text: A nightly job applies merged changes and opens tickets for any detected drift

options.name: reconciler
options.text: A controller inside each environment continuously reconciles live state to the repository contents

options.name: manualapply
options.text: Engineers run apply locally from a locked state backend after a reviewed plan

options.name: ciapply
options.text: A pipeline holding production credentials applies each reviewed plan automatically after merge

decision: How should the team handle tests that fail intermittently in CI?
context: A 9-engineer team runs 4,200 tests in a 14-minute CI pipeline, and about 1.5% of runs fail on non-deterministic tests. Around 60% of those failures come from one integration suite that exercises redelivery behavior against a real message-broker container. Engineers re-run red builds by hand about 20 times a week.

options.name: quarantine
options.text: Move flaky tests to a non-blocking quarantine suite, with a ticket per test

options.name: autoretry
options.text: Retry failed tests automatically up to three times before marking the build red

options.name: stopline
options.text: Pause merges whenever a flaky test appears until its root cause is fixed

options.name: fakebroker
options.text: Swap the real broker container in that suite for an in-memory test double

decision: How should the browser end-to-end tests run in the delivery pipeline?
context: A web product has 180 Playwright tests that take 35 minutes serially, or 9 minutes on 8 parallel runners costing about 400 dollars a month. The team merges around 25 pull requests a day, and two production regressions last quarter came from flows that only the end-to-end suite covers.

options.name: smokepr
options.text: Run 20 critical-path tests on each pull request and the full suite nightly

options.name: everypr
options.text: Run the full suite on every pull request and require it to pass

options.name: riskbased
options.text: Run the full suite on pull requests that touch code paths labelled high-risk

options.name: aftermerge
options.text: Run the full suite after each merge to main and revert on failure

decision: What release cadence should the B2B web app adopt?
context: A 14-person team ships a web app to about 300 customer accounts, and several of them run quarterly acceptance checks and ask for advance notice of visible UI changes. Each release currently takes 3 hours of manual verification by two engineers, and there is no automated rollback. Most features change both the backend and the UI in the same pull request.

options.name: train
options.text: Ship on a fixed two-week train with a changelog published to customers beforehand

options.name: continuous
options.text: Deploy every merged change to production automatically, hiding visible changes behind dark launches

options.name: splitlane
options.text: Deploy backend changes continuously and batch customer-visible UI changes into a monthly release

options.name: ondemand
options.text: Release whenever a feature is complete, verified by the engineer who built it

decision: What recovery policy should production releases follow?
context: The service deploys 3 times a day, and 40% of releases include a schema migration that cannot be reversed without losing data. Reverting the application image takes 4 minutes, while forward fixes have averaged 35 minutes, and about half of new features sit behind flags.

options.name: flagoff
options.text: Switch off the responsible feature flag first, then ship a corrective release later

options.name: revert
options.text: Roll back to the previous image at once and debug the failure on staging

options.name: splitmigrate
options.text: Ship schema migrations in a separate weekly release, decoupled from ordinary application deploys

options.name: forward
options.text: Write and deploy a forward fix on top of the already-migrated schema

decision: How should pull requests be approved before merging?
context: An 8-engineer team merges about 30 pull requests a week, with a median review wait of 19 hours. Two of the last five incidents traced to changes that a single reviewer approved quickly, and one of them was in code outside the areas the team treats as high-risk. Three engineers work 8 hours behind the other five.

options.name: tiered
options.text: Require one approval by default and two for changes touching auth, billing or schema

options.name: onereview
options.text: Require one approval from any teammate, with a two-hour response target for reviewers

options.name: postmerge
options.text: Merge after green CI, then review within 24 hours and revert on objection

options.name: tworeview
options.text: Require two approvals on every pull request, one of them from the owning area

decision: How should the large module refactor be reviewed and merged?
context: A refactor touches 140 files across 6 modules and produces a 4,500-line diff, of which about 85% is mechanical renames and import moves. Only two engineers know the affected modules well, and four other engineers have open branches in those modules. The release freeze starts in three weeks.

options.name: walkthrough
options.text: Hold a live walkthrough with both module experts and approve the full diff together

options.name: codemod
options.text: Land the renames first as a scripted change, then review logic edits separately

options.name: integration
options.text: Merge module by module into an integration branch, reviewing each module's changes there

options.name: stacked
options.text: Split the work into a stack of small pull requests merged in dependency order

decision: How should the React dashboard manage data fetched from the API?
context: A 7-developer team maintains a React dashboard with 40 screens backed by 25 REST endpoints. About 70% of its state is server data shared across screens, and the rest is form state and UI toggles. Today every request is a hand-written Redux thunk with its own loading flags, and about 300 components read from Redux selectors.

options.name: keepthunks
options.text: Keep the existing thunks and add a normalized entity cache with typed selectors

options.name: tanstack
options.text: Adopt TanStack Query for server data and keep Redux only for client state

options.name: contexthooks
options.text: Replace Redux with React context and custom hooks wrapping plain fetch calls

options.name: rtkquery
options.text: Migrate every request to RTK Query endpoints inside the existing Redux store

decision: How should the public product pages be rendered?
context: A catalogue site has 60,000 product pages, and prices change on about 10% of them each hour; stale prices have caused refund requests. Organic search brings 55% of traffic, and the 6-person team knows React but has never operated server-side rendering in production.

options.name: isr
options.text: Generate static pages and regenerate each in the background every few minutes

options.name: islands
options.text: Use Astro islands, hydrating only the price and cart components in the browser

options.name: ssr
options.text: Render each page on the server per request, behind a short CDN cache

options.name: staticshell
options.text: Serve static HTML for each product and fetch live prices in the browser

decision: How should the public API's list endpoints paginate?
context: The orders endpoint holds 80 million rows, gains about 200 new rows per second, and an exact count on it takes about 4 seconds. Roughly 5,000 partner integrations call the API, some rendering numbered page links in their UIs and others syncing everything overnight.

options.name: keyset
options.text: Keyset pagination on created time and id, exposed as plain query parameters

options.name: dualmode
options.text: Support both cursors for bulk sync and capped page numbers for display use cases

options.name: offsetcap
options.text: Offset and limit parameters, with offsets beyond 10,000 rejected by the server

options.name: opaque
options.text: Opaque cursor tokens returned with each page and valid for 24 hours

decision: Which API style should the new mobile and partner backend expose?
context: Clients are two native mobile apps and about 40 partner systems built by outside teams on slow-moving enterprise stacks. Mobile screens now need 4 to 6 REST calls each, and the 5-engineer backend team has no GraphQL experience.

options.name: bff
options.text: Keep REST for partners and build a separate backend-for-frontend for the mobile apps

options.name: composite
options.text: Keep resource-oriented REST with OpenAPI docs and add composite endpoints for heavy mobile screens

options.name: graphql
options.text: Expose one GraphQL schema to every client, with persisted queries for the mobile apps

options.name: sparse
options.text: Keep REST but add field selection and relationship expansion parameters to existing resources

decision: How should known-vulnerable dependencies be handled in CI?
context: A Node service has about 900 transitive dependencies, and the audit tool reports 31 advisories, 4 of them rated high and none shown to be reachable from the service's code. The service ships twice a day, and the 7-person team has one engineer who handles security part time.

options.name: reachable
options.text: Fail the build only when reachability analysis shows the vulnerable function is called

options.name: autopatch
options.text: Enable automated update pull requests for every advisory and merge them when tests pass

options.name: gate
options.text: Fail the build on any high or critical advisory unless a waiver exists

options.name: deadlines
options.text: Open a ticket per advisory with severity-based patch deadlines and leave builds ungated

decision: Where should scanning for committed credentials run?
context: A 12-person team pushes about 150 commits a day and has leaked an API key twice in two years, each time revoked within an hour with no misuse found. Some contributors use personal machines where hooks cannot be enforced, and the hosting plan's built-in push protection costs 21 dollars per seat per month.

options.name: nightly
options.text: A nightly scan of the full repository history that alerts on each new finding

options.name: pushprotect
options.text: Server-side push protection that rejects pushes containing common secret formats before they land

options.name: precommit
options.text: A pre-commit hook on each developer machine that blocks commits containing known credential patterns

options.name: cijob
options.text: A CI scan of each pull request's diff that fails the check on matches

decision: How should on-call duty be organized for the product team?
context: Five engineers own 9 services and receive about 6 pages a week, 40% of them outside business hours. Two engineers know the billing service well, the other three have never handled its alerts, and two of the five have caregiving duties that make overnight weeks hard.

options.name: ownership
options.text: Per-service ownership, where each engineer is paged only for the two services they own

options.name: weekly
options.text: One weekly rotation across all five engineers, with a runbook for each service

options.name: outsourced
options.text: A business-hours team rotation, with a contracted vendor triaging overnight pages and escalating

options.name: pairing
options.text: A weekly rotation with a primary and a secondary who shadows each page

decision: How should the team allocate time to technical debt?
context: A 10-engineer team works in 2-week sprints and has 45 open debt tickets, the oldest 18 months old. Two customer-facing launches are committed for next quarter, and velocity has dropped about 15% in a year, which engineers attribute to slow builds and a tangled billing module.

options.name: rotation
options.text: Rotate one engineer onto debt work full time each sprint, ranked by team vote

options.name: fixedshare
options.text: Reserve 20% of every sprint's capacity for debt tickets that engineers choose

options.name: boyscout
options.text: Fix debt inside modules a feature already touches, and include it in the estimate

options.name: hardening
options.text: Schedule a hardening sprint after every fifth feature sprint, with no feature work
